chapter: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
title: Charlie Shavers's technique and unrecognized warmth
summary: Leeman sums up how Dorsey grew to love Shavers, who lived near him in Corona, and regrets that Shavers's technical brilliance and early death kept him from full recognition.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: To sum up Tommy Dorsey and my association with him, after so many years of evading integration in his band -- instrumentalists, that is -- Tommy Dorsey grew to love Charlie Shavers as a most beautiful and unusual human being, which he was. To say nothing of his awe of Charlie's vast technique on the trumpet, as well as his wonderful warmth and beauty of his playing that he added to the band. Tommy had those attributes on trombone -- technically and

warmth in his playing. And I, among others, never considered him a jazz player -- his idol was Jack Teagarden. I can't recall working with Charlie Shavers again after that episode, although we were real fond of each other and saw a lot of each other constantly in New York. He only lived 5 minutes away from me in Corona. And two or three blocks from Louis Armstrong.

I'd go into clubs like the Metro in New York to say hello and Charlie had a quartet there, and several other places, and I would listen to him and he would have me over for barbecue occasionally, and we were in close touch until his death. His death was premature. He had had many illness including diabetes, he wouldn't stop drinking or taking doctor's orders. I don't think Charlie was given full evaluation of his warmth and his beauty, because he had intertwined a great deal of technique in his jazz performances, and it might have turned some people off -- I don't know why, possibly they were jealous, because the warmth was there and the swinging was there.

Today one of the greatest trumpet players alive to me is Clark Terry. He's accepted as such, and I don't think critics of musicians put him down for his great technical prowress and swinging. Maybe Charlie didn't live long enough to enjoy the fulfillment and acceptance of his greatness, along his technical lines and
so forth -- as people admire that today, too, along with a person's swinging.
